new_statements.quote: En tzotzil existen dos tipos de acentuación prosódica: A. Las palabras se acentúan sobre la primera sílaba de la raíz, sea ésta simple o compuesta. En cadenas de varias sílabas se acentúa otra sílaba más, de manera que nunca aparezcan más de tres sílabas seguidas sin acento. Ejemplos: cha.c'ü.xu.bi.nún.cu.tíc ustedes tienen misericordia de nosotros / li.vï.ni.que.ti.qué los hombres [...] B. La última sílaba de una oración se acentúa con un aumento en el tono de la última sílaba y un desvanecimiento del mismo. [...] Por el hecho de que la acentuación obedece estas reglas, no es necesario indicarla en forma escrita en el idioma.
new_statements.translation: In Tzotzil there are two types of prosodic accentuation: A. Words are accented on the first syllable of the root, whether it is simple or compound. In strings of several syllables one more syllable is accented, so that never more than three syllables in a row appear without accent. Examples: cha.c'ü.xu.bi.nún.cu.tíc 'you (pl.) have mercy on us' / li.vï.ni.que.ti.qué 'the men' [...] B. The last syllable of a sentence is accented with a rise in the pitch of that last syllable and a fading of it. [...] Because accentuation obeys these rules, it is not necessary to mark it in the written language.

Serie de Vocabularios y Diccionarios Indígenas 'Mariano Silva y Aceves' 22. México, D.F.: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano / Secretaría de Educación Pública.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent falls on the first syllable of the root (not of the word: prefixes such as cha-, li-, s- are unaccented), for simple and compound roots alike; in long words a further rhythmic accent is added so that no more than three unaccented syllables run together (the printed examples show the extra accents on later suffix syllables). Separately, the final syllable of a sentence carries a rising-then-falling pitch prominence, and the final syllable of a preceding subordinate clause or noun phrase a rise without fall. Accent is fully predictable and is not.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'en cadenas de varias sílabas se acentúa otra sílaba más, de manera que nunca aparezcan más de tres sílabas seguidas sin acento' — an additional (rhythmic) accent in longer words; in the examples the root-initial syllable is printed with diaeresis (c'ü, vï) and the added accents with acute (nún, tíc; qué), so cha.c'ü.xu.bi.nún.cu.tíc has the root accent on c'u(xubin) and extra accents on nun and tic.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for the word level. The phrase-level rule (B) puts prominence on the final syllable of a sentence or of a preceding subordinate clause / NP, which can differ from the root-initial word accent (example: Mi ta xabát oc'obë, chajchí'inöt). Laughlin 1975 (Zinacantán) adds that words in isolation take final stress except affective -luh verbs, 1pl.excl suffixes and disyllabic reduplicated stems; the San Andrés source does not mention these.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (rule A, stated over words including compounds) versus sentence/clause level (rule B, pitch-based prominence on the final syllable of a sentence or preceding clause/NP). Rule A is the lexical word-stress rule; rule B is intonational. Nothing said about citation forms in isolation (Laughlin 1975 and Haviland 1981, both Zinacantán, treat isolated words as phrase-final and hence final-stressed).
new_statements.identity_note: tzot1260 is a Bookkeeping node for the San Andrés Larráinzar dialect of Tzotzil (ISO tzs, merged into tzo in 2008 by ISO change request 2008-061); the language-level code is tzot1259 (Tzotzil). The quoted source, Delgaty & Ruiz Sánchez 1978, describes exactly the San Andrés (Larráinzar) variety, with dialect variants noted from Chamula, Chenalhó, Huixtán, Zinacantán etc; its grammar part was written by Marion Cowan with San Andrés examples checked by a Chenalhó speaker. The Zinacantán descriptions held by the project (Laughlin 1975 p. 23; Haviland 1981 p. 14) state the same root-initial word accent plus phrase-final prominence, so the rule appears to be pan-Tzotzil rather than dialect-specific; the -luh / 1pl.excl / reduplication exceptions for isolated words are stated only for Zinacantán.

sources.citation: Bennett, Ryan. 2016. Mayan phonology. Language and Linguistics Compass 10(10): 469-514.
sources.note: Survey; §6.1 notes that phonetic correlates of stress in Mayan are underdocumented and that Herrera Zendejas (2014) gives limited instrumental data on Tsotsil stress; §6.2 discusses reported tone in San Bartolo (Venustiano Carranza) Tsotsil (Sarles 1966). No San Andrés-specific stress statement.

sources.citation: Haviland, John B. 1981. Sk'op sotz'leb: El tzotzil de San Lorenzo Zinacantán. México: UNAM, Instituto de Investigaciones Filológicas, Centro de Estudios Mayas. Capítulo I 'Notas sobre la fonología', pp. 7-19.
sources.note: p. 14 (Zinacantán dialect): 'El acento primario de una palabra tzotzil cae en la primera sílaba de la raíz; además hay un acento aun más fuerte que acompaña la última sílaba de una frase o una oración..'; particles are unaccented unless phrase-final. Same rule as the San Andrés source, different dialect.

sources.citation: Laughlin, Robert M. 1975. The Great Tzotzil Dictionary of San Lorenzo Zinacantán. Smithsonian Contributions to Anthropology 19. Washington: Smithsonian Institution Press. p. 23 (Explanatory notes).
sources.note: p. 23: 'Primary stress occurs on the final syllable of single words in isolation except in affective verbs with -luh, first person plural exclusive suffixes, and reduplicated stems of two syllables.. In normal speech, however, primary stress falls upon the root vowels (on the first, if there are two) and at the end of a phrase.' Zinacantán dialect; this is the source of the Wikipedia paragraph the earlier scan relied on.
